items.title: Dr. Carla Hayden: “The Future of Libraries is About More Than Books”
items.raw_text: From a New Op/Ed by Dr. Carla Hayden on Time Magazine/Time.com: Dr. Carla Hayden Historically, libraries have served as a crucial part of the cultural and civic infrastructure of the nation, responding to local needs and bringing the world to people of all ages. However, in many places today, libraries and library workers are under attack . These attacks are echoes of the past, yet contain a new intensity when libraries are one of the only places where people can go for accurate information and inspiration, while also providing an all-important and free-of-cost “ third space ” between work and home. As the 14th Librarian of Congress, as a Senior Fellow at Mellon, and as a librarian whose career spans several decades among various types of libraries, I’ve had the opportunity to work and engage with library workers in all positions. One thing that becomes clear when you talk to librarians today is that libraries must embed themselves in the community, and the community in them. The institutions that will survive are the ones that let their communities shape them. Across fields, library and cultural workers are taking stock of local experts and leaders, leveraging their libraries as a convener and curator of their local community and its residents. items.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
items.raw_text: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering. The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says. Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks. Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted. items.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
items.raw_text: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. items.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
items.raw_text: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

items.raw_text: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.raw_text: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. items.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
items.raw_text: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. items.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
items.raw_text: NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon. The moves were designed to give the agency's lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit. These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. items.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
items.raw_text: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack. items.title: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits
items.raw_text: A Ukrainian barrage of missiles and drones collapsed a crucial segment of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Strait Bridge—and Ukraine’s military pulled off the strike deep within Russian-occupied territory without relying on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications to guide the missiles in. On the nights of November 15 and November 16, coordinated waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles caused enough damage to collapse one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch bridge’s roadway for automobile traffic, according to an Institute for the Study of War update . Russian sources claimed several hundred Ukrainian drones first overwhelmed Russian air defenses to pave the way for remote-controlled missile strikes focused on the bridge, with the latter prominently including Ukraine’s homegrown Flamingo cruise missile. The Ukrainian operation adapted a Russian battlefield innovation by using drones equipped with mesh radios to create an airborne communications network, according to the Financial Times . Each networked drone acts as a relay node to extend the communication link between human operators and remotely piloted missiles and strike drones. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings. After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it " shameful " and a " national embarrassment ." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week. But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. items.title: Spoelstra Spreekt: Trein gemist
items.raw_text: COLUMN – Ik moet een nieuwe telefoon. Mijn huidige telefoon is inmiddels acht jaar oud, dus dat heb ik best knap gedaan. In de tussentijd hebben mijn kinderen al minimaal zes keer hun toestel vervangen. Ook omdat ze die dingen om de drie dagen laten vallen en elk half jaar kwijt zijn. En nu ben ik aan de beurt. Op zich ben ik nog best tevreden maar hij wordt steeds trager. Voordeel is dat ik ook steeds trager word, dus ik merk het eigenlijk amper. Ik wil ook helemaal geen nieuwe telefoon maar ik word min of meer gedwongen. Vernieuwen is nu eenmaal het verdienmodel in de ict. Ik sprak van de week een eigenaar van een kantoorautomatiseringsbedrijfje. Ik vroeg of hij het druk had. Hij zei: nou het is veel rustiger dan vorig jaar. Toen hebben we het heel druk gehad (lees: heel veel geld verdiend) met de overgang naar Windows 11 . Hij zei er ook achteraan: ik kan niet wachten op Windows 12. En natuurlijk komt er een Windows 12. Lang gaat dat niet duren. En er komt ook zeker een 13 en 14. Dit is nu eenmaal de tijd waarin we leven. We kunnen nooit eens zeggen: dit is het. Van nu af aan werken we zo en de rest van ons leven ook. Sinds de industriële revolutie hebben we een mechanisme in gang gezet waarbij we constant willen automatiseren. Er rijdt een trein en daar moeten we opstappen. Niemand wil die trein missen want je wilt niet op het perron staan en nog net in de verte de achterlichten zien verdwijnen. Nu stappen we weer allemaal op de ai-trein. Waar de trein naartoe gaat maakt

items.title: Dit zijn de winnaars van de Computable Awards 2026
items.raw_text: De winnaars van de Computable Awards 2026 zijn bekend. Tijdens een feestelijke gala-avond in De Polar in Jaarbeurs Utrecht zijn dinsdagavond 17 november zeventien awards uitgereikt aan bedrijven, organisaties en ict-professionals die zich onderscheiden met innovatieve projecten en bijzondere prestaties. De Lifetime Achievement Award ging dit jaar naar ict-ondernemer Eugène Tuijnman. De 21e editie van de Computable Awards stond in het teken van Pushing Boundaries . Onder leiding van presentatrice Anic van Damme werden de prijzen uitgereikt in vier thematische blokken: Autonomous Trust, Human Authority, Intelligent Transformation en Resilient Futures. De winnaars laten zien hoe breed de Nederlandse ict-sector zich ontwikkelt. Van ai die familiegesprekken op de intensive care begrijpelijker maakt tot een Europees alternatief voor Amerikaanse kantoorsoftware. En van cybersecurity voor ruim 180 bedrijven tot een dataplatform dat The Ocean Cleanup ondersteunt bij het bestrijden van plasticvervuiling. Lifetime Achievement Award voor Eugène Tuijnman Een bijzonder moment van de avond was de uitreiking van de Lifetime Achievement Award aan Eugène Tuijnman. De oprichter van ict-dienstverlener SLTN ontvangt de onderscheiding voor zijn jarenlange bijdrage aan de Nederlandse ict-sector. Tuijnman richtte SLTN bijna dertig jaar geleden op en bouwde de onderneming uit tot een van de grotere zelfstandige ict-dienstverleners van Nederland.
